summary: Specifies the CLEFIA block cipher, which works on 128-bit blocks with key lengths of 128, 192 and 256 bits and has the same interface as AES. It was published in 2007 and is designed to be lightweight. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A recipe for scrambling messages in fixed-size chunks so only someone with the key can unscramble them. It is another recipe like AES.

questions: lightweight block cipher for constrained devices
subtitle: A lightweight block cipher for constrained devices.

tldr.problem: Devices with limited hardware resources, such as wireless sensors, need encryption but current block ciphers like AES are too large to implement efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: CLEFIA is a 128-bit block cipher that uses generalized Feistel networks and two types of S-boxes combined with diffusion matrices to encrypt data with 128, 192, or 256-bit keys, all while requiring minimal hardware gates.
tldr.outcome: CLEFIA can be implemented in about 3,000 logic gates on a standard chip, making it practical for resource-constrained devices while maintaining strong security with no known weaknesses since 2007.

today: RFC 6114 is an Informational RFC that specifies CLEFIA. The cipher remains widely recognized as a secure lightweight option for constrained environments, appearing in international standards and recommended cipher lists.

sections.title: Why Lightweight Cryptography Matters
sections.content:
As the Internet expands to connect resource-constrained devices like wireless sensors and remote monitors, these devices need to protect their communications with encryption. Traditional block ciphers like the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) require substantial hardware resources: they need thousands of transistor gates and consume significant power. CLEFIA addresses this problem by offering a block cipher designed from the ground up to work efficiently on constrained hardware while preserving strong security.

CLEFIA was published in 2007 and has since been scrutinized in the academic community with no significant security weaknesses discovered. It is currently a lightweight option in the ISO/IEC 29192-2 standard and the CRYPTREC project for recommended Japanese government ciphers.
sections.eli5: When you have a tiny device that needs to send secret messages but does not have much computer power, it needs a special encryption recipe that works with fewer transistors and less energy.

sections.title: The CLEFIA Algorithm Structure
sections.content:
CLEFIA is a 128-bit block cipher, meaning it processes data in 128-bit (16-byte) chunks. It accepts keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits and produces a ciphertext block of the same size as the plaintext block, matching the interface of AES for compatibility. The algorithm has two main parts: the data processing part and the key scheduling part.

The data processing uses a generalized Feistel network (GFN), a structure where data flows through multiple rounds of transformation. In CLEFIA's case, a 4-branch GFN is used, dividing the 128-bit block into four 32-bit words that are processed in parallel through 18, 22, or 26 rounds, depending on the key size. Each round applies two F-functions, which take one of the words and a round key to produce a value that is XORed (combined bitwise) with another word.
sections.eli5: CLEFIA splits the message into four equal pieces and mixes them together in many rounds. Each round uses a special mixing function and a different part of the secret key to scramble the pieces.

sections.title: Building Blocks: S-Boxes and Diffusion Matrices
sections.content:
The F-functions that process each word are built from two types of 8-bit S-boxes (substitution boxes), called S0 and S1. S-boxes are lookup tables that take an 8-bit input and produce an 8-bit output; they provide the nonlinear transformation that prevents simple mathematical attacks. S0 is constructed from four 4-bit S-boxes, while S1 is based on the inverse function over the finite field GF(2^8).

After the S-boxes, the output passes through a diffusion matrix (either M0 or M1, depending on which F-function is used) that mixes the bytes together. These matrices multiply the output bytes in the finite field GF(2^8) using constants like 0x02, 0x04, 0x06, 0x08, and 0x0a. This diffusion ensures that changing a single input bit affects multiple output bits, preventing attacks that exploit patterns.
sections.eli5: Lookup tables scramble the numbers in a nonlinear way, then matrices spread out the changes so that one small change in input scrambles the whole output.

sections.title: Key Scheduling and Whitening Keys
sections.content:
Before encrypting data, CLEFIA performs key scheduling to generate whitening keys and round keys. Whitening keys are XORed with the data before the first round and after the last round for additional security. Round keys are used in each round of the Feistel network.

For 128-bit keys, CLEFIA first generates an intermediate key L using a 12-round generalized Feistel network with constant values. For 192-bit and 256-bit keys, it uses a larger 8-branch, 10-round GFN to produce two intermediate values. These intermediate values and the original key are then expanded to produce all the whitening and round keys needed for encryption. The constant values used in key scheduling are derived from the mathematical constants e (the base of natural logarithm, 2.71828...) and pi (3.14159...).
sections.eli5: Before encrypting, the secret key is processed to create many different round keys, each used in a different part of the encryption to make sure the key cannot be guessed.

sections.title: Lightweight Implementation and Security
sections.content:
CLEFIA achieves its lightweight design through careful engineering. A hardware implementation requires only about 3,000 logic gates using a standard 0.13-micrometer CMOS library, making it significantly smaller than AES while maintaining strong performance in both hardware and software. This compact size does not compromise security: the 128-bit block size and key sizes (128, 192, or 256 bits) provide security levels of 128, 192, and 256 bits respectively.

The security of CLEFIA has been evaluated through multiple channels. The designers have published cryptanalysis results, and independent cryptographers have scrutinized the algorithm since publication in 2007. To date, no practical security weaknesses have been found for the full-round version. CLEFIA's use in ISO/IEC 29192-2 and CRYPTREC reflects international confidence in its security as a lightweight cipher suitable for resource-constrained Internet-connected devices.
sections.eli5: CLEFIA fits in very little computer hardware but still uses strong encryption that has been tested for many years without anyone finding a way to break it.
